claim: Müller glia extend fine filopodia-like processes into retinal synaptic layers.
source: Müller glia extend fine filopodia-like processes into retinal synaptic layers, in similar fashion to brain astrocytes and radial glia that exhibit perisynaptic processes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of Müller glia morphology.

claim: During the second postnatal week, Müller glial processes were highly dynamic, with rapid extensions and retractions.
source: Using two-photon volumetric imaging, we found that during the second postnatal week, Müller glial processes were highly dynamic, with rapid extensions and retractions that were mediated by cytoskeletal rearrangements.
evidence: This finding is based on two-photon volumetric imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Müller glial process motility was mediated by cytoskeletal rearrangements.
source: Using two-photon volumetric imaging, we found that during the second postnatal week, Müller glial processes were highly dynamic, with rapid extensions and retractions that were mediated by cytoskeletal rearrangements.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that cytoskeletal disrupting agents affected motility.

claim: Retinal waves led to increases in cytosolic calcium within Müller glial lateral processes and stalks.
source: During this same stage of development, retinal waves led to increases in cytosolic calcium within Müller glial lateral processes and stalks.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Müller glial stalks and lateral processes comprised distinct calcium compartments.
source: These regions comprised distinct calcium compartments, distinguished by variable participation in waves, timing, and sensitivity to an M1 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing differential responses to pharmacological manipulations.

claim: Motility of lateral processes was unaffected by pharmacological agents that enhanced or blocked wave-associated calcium transients.
source: However, we found that motility of lateral processes was unaffected by the presence of pharmacological agents that enhanced or blocked wave-associated calcium transients.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from pharmacological manipulations combined with motility imaging.

claim: Mice lacking normal cholinergic waves in the first postnatal week exhibited normal Müller glial process morphology.
source: Finally, we found that mice lacking normal cholinergic waves in the first postnatal week also exhibited normal Müller glial process morphology.
evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of β2-nAChR-KO mice.

claim: Outgrowth of Müller glial lateral processes into synaptic layers is determined by factors that are independent of neuronal activity.
source: Hence, outgrowth of Müller glial lateral processes into synaptic layers is determined by factors that are independent of neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing lack of effect of neuronal activity manipulations on process morphology.

claim: Müller glia exhibit neurogenic potential.
source: In the vertebrate retina, for example, Müller glia exhibit neurogenic potential (Bernardos et al., 2007; Ji et al., 2017; Guimarães et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Müller glia promote circuit-specific wiring via secretion of synaptogenic molecules.
source: promote circuit-specific wiring via secretion of synaptogenic molecules (Koh et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Müller glia regulate phagocytosis of neuronal debris.
source: regulate phagocytosis of neuronal debris (Bejarano-Escobar et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Müller glia limit neurotransmitter spillover via transporter activity.
source: and limit neurotransmitter spillover via transporter activity (Bringmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Individual astroglia extend fine processes that contact thousands of synapses.
source: Individual astroglia extend fine processes that contact thousands of synapses and express an array of neurotransmitter receptors (Allen and Eroglu, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Neuronal activity-evoked calcium events in astroglia range in size from small membrane-proximal microdomains to global cytosolic events.
source: Neuronal activity-evoked calcium events in astroglia range in size from small membrane-proximal microdomains to global cytosolic events mediated by various transmembrane proteins and calcium sources (Shigetomi et al., 2016; Bindocci et al., 2017; Nimmerjahn and Bergles, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Compartmentalized and global calcium events in astroglia are mediated by separate mechanisms.
source: Pharmacological studies suggest compartmentalized and global calcium events are mediated by separate mechanisms and evoke different functional responses within astroglia, which lead to differential effects on neurotransmission (Di Castro et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2020; Srinivasan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous pharmacological studies.

claim: Müller glia are the predominant glial type in the retina.
source: In the retina, Müller glia are the predominant glial type, tiling the entire retinal space and interacting with every retinal cell type (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Müller glia exhibit a radial structure with a stalk extending from the soma, lateral processes extending from the stalk within synaptic layers, and endfeet contacting neuronal somata, axons, and vasculature.
source: Similar to Bergmann glia of the cerebellum (De Zeeuw and Hoogland, 2015; Lippman et al., 2008), Müller glia exhibit a radial structure with a stalk extending from the soma, lateral processes extending from the stalk within synaptic layers, and endfeet contacting neuronal somata, axons, and vasculature.
evidence: This is a description of Müller glia morphology supported by citations.

claim: Müller glia undergo calcium transients in response to retinal waves during mouse development.
source: During both mouse (Rosa et al., 2015) and zebrafish (Zhang et al., 2019) development, Müller glia undergo calcium transients in response to retinal waves
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Müller glia undergo calcium transients in response to retinal waves during zebrafish development.
source: During both mouse (Rosa et al., 2015) and zebrafish (Zhang et al., 2019) development, Müller glia undergo calcium transients in response to retinal waves
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The functional relevance of wave-associated calcium signaling in Müller glia is not known.
source: The functional relevance of wave-associated calcium signaling in Müller glia is not known.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Outgrowth of Müller glial lateral processes initiates and progresses during the same developmental window as retinal waves.
source: One potential role for wave-associated calcium-signaling in Müller glia is in modulating outgrowth of lateral processes, which initiates and progresses during the same developmental window as retinal waves (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the hippocampus and somatosensory cortex, perisynaptic astrocytic processes undergo spatially localized, glutamate-evoked calcium transients which are essential for activity-evoked ensheathment of synapses.
source: For example, in the hippocampus and somatosensory cortex, perisynaptic astrocytic processes undergo spatially localized, glutamate-evoked calcium transients which are essential for activity-evoked ensheathment of synapses (Bernardinelli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Bergmann glial processes are highly motile during synaptogenic periods.
source: In the cerebellum, Bergmann glial processes are highly motile during synaptogenic periods, and their ensheathment of Purkinje cells is impaired when glial glutamate transporters are knocked out (Lippman et al., 2008; Miyazaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ensheathment of Purkinje cells by Bergmann glia is impaired when glial glutamate transporters are knocked out.
source: In the cerebellum, Bergmann glial processes are highly motile during synaptogenic periods, and their ensheathment of Purkinje cells is impaired when glial glutamate transporters are knocked out (Lippman et al., 2008; Miyazaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Radial glia of the Xenopus optic tectum exhibit neuronal activity-evoked calcium transients and motility during visual system development.
source: Radial glia of the Xenopus optic tectum exhibit neuronal activity-evoked calcium transients and motility during visual system development (Sild et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: When glial motility is blocked, synaptic development, function, and plasticity are impaired.
source: In many of these systems, when glial motility is blocked, synaptic development, function, and plasticity are impaired (Van Horn and Ruthazer, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Müller glia differentiate from retinal progenitor cells during the first postnatal week.
source: After their differentiation from retinal progenitor cells, which occurs during the first postnatal week, Müller glia extend processes laterally from their stalk into the inner plexiform layer (IPL) (MacDonald et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Müller glia extend processes laterally from their stalk into the inner plexiform layer (IPL) after differentiation.
source: After their differentiation from retinal progenitor cells, which occurs during the first postnatal week, Müller glia extend processes laterally from their stalk into the inner plexiform layer (IPL) (MacDonald et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Lateral processes exhibited sublayer-specific outgrowth and distribution.
source: Lateral processes exhibited sublayer-specific outgrowth and distribution, and they reached an adult level of complexity soon after eye opening around postnatal day 14 (P14) (Figure 1B and D; see Supplementary files 1 and 2 for statistical comparisons across sublayer and age, respectively).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 1B and D with statistical analysis.

claim: Müller glial lateral processes reached an adult level of complexity soon after eye opening around postnatal day 14 (P14).
source: Lateral processes exhibited sublayer-specific outgrowth and distribution, and they reached an adult level of complexity soon after eye opening around postnatal day 14 (P14) (Figure 1B and D; see Supplementary files 1 and 2 for statistical comparisons across sublayer and age, respectively).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 1B and D with statistical analysis.

claim: During the first days of Müller glia differentiation, lateral processes preferentially occupied the borders of the IPL (putative S1/S5).
source: During the first days of Müller glia differentiation, lateral processes preferentially occupied the borders of the IPL (putative S1/S5), with most outgrowth occurring in the prospective ON half of the IPL (S3–S5) until about P10.
evidence: This is based on observational data from imaging experiments.

claim: Most outgrowth of Müller glial lateral processes occurred in the prospective ON half of the IPL (S3–S5) until about P10.
source: During the first days of Müller glia differentiation, lateral processes preferentially occupied the borders of the IPL (putative S1/S5), with most outgrowth occurring in the prospective ON half of the IPL (S3–S5) until about P10.
evidence: This is based on observational data from imaging experiments.

claim: By eye opening, after P12, Müller glial processes arborized throughout the IPL and began to resemble their adult distribution.
source: By eye opening, after P12, processes arborized throughout the IPL and began to resemble their adult distribution, characterized by fewer processes in IPL sublayers S2/S4 than in S1/S3/S5.
evidence: This is based on observational data from imaging experiments.

claim: Adult Müller glial process distribution is characterized by fewer processes in IPL sublayers S2/S4 than in S1/S3/S5.
source: By eye opening, after P12, processes arborized throughout the IPL and began to resemble their adult distribution, characterized by fewer processes in IPL sublayers S2/S4 than in S1/S3/S5.
evidence: This is based on observational data from imaging experiments.

claim: The observations of Müller glial process development are consistent with previous findings using the same mouse line and immunohistochemistry in fixed tissue.
source: These observations are consistent with previous findings using the same mouse line and immunohistochemistry in fixed tissue (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previous study cited.

claim: Müller glial cell lateral processes were highly motile across the IPL throughout the entire second postnatal week.
source: First, Müller glial cell lateral processes were highly motile across the IPL throughout the entire second postnatal week.
evidence: This is based on volumetric two-photon imaging data.

claim: There was a slight bias toward new process sprouting rather than process loss during the second postnatal week.
source: Second, there was a slight bias toward new process sprouting rather than process loss.
evidence: This is based on analysis of motility imaging data.

claim: There were roughly equal proportions of extending and retracting Müller glial processes over 10-min epochs of imaging.
source: Third, we found there were roughly equal proportions of extending and retracting processes over 10-min epochs of imaging, highlighting their rapid turnover during this period of development.
evidence: This is based on analysis of motility imaging data.

claim: There was a sharp developmental transition toward stability in Müller glial lateral processes a few days after eye opening.
source: Finally, we observed a sharp developmental transition toward stability a few days after eye opening (Figure 1C, E and F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 1C, E, and F with statistical analysis.

claim: Process motility was reduced by bath application of the microtubule-disrupting agent nocodazole (10 µM) and the actin polymerization inhibitor cytochalasin-D (5 µM).
source: Process motility was reduced by bath application of the microtubule-disrupting agent nocodazole (10 µM) and the actin polymerization inhibitor cytochalasin-D (5 µM), the combination of which led to processes stabilization (Figure 1G; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological manipulation experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The combination of nocodazole and cytochalasin-D led to Müller glial process stabilization.
source: Process motility was reduced by bath application of the microtubule-disrupting agent nocodazole (10 µM) and the actin polymerization inhibitor cytochalasin-D (5 µM), the combination of which led to processes stabilization (Figure 1G; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological manipulation experiments shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Müller glial process morphology remained normal in the presence of cytochalasin and nocodazole.
source: It is unlikely that this loss of motility resulted from damaged cell health, as Müller glial process morphology remained normal in the presence of cytochalasin and nocodazole.
evidence: This is based on observational data from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: Müller glia exhibit reactive gliosis associated with hypertrophy and expression of filamentous membrane processes when exposed to damage.
source: Müller glia, like astroglia throughout the brain, exhibit reactive gliosis associated with hypertrophy and expression of filamentous membrane processes when exposed to damage (Graca et al., 2018), which we did not observe here.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study and used as a control observation.

claim: Bath application of epidermal growth factor (EGF; one unit [100 ng]/ml) enhanced Müller glial process motility.
source: Second, we enhanced process motility by bath application of epidermal growth factor (EGF; one unit [100 ng]/ml; Figure 1H; Supplementary file 5), which activates EGF receptors (EGFRs).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological manipulation experiments shown in Figure 1H.

claim: EGFRs are expressed by Müller glia during the second postnatal week.
source: EGFRs are expressed by Müller glia during the second postnatal week (Close et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: EGFRs increase motility in other cells via activation of Rac- and Rho-GTPase-dependent pathways.
source: and increase motility in other cells via activation of Rac- and Rho-GTPase-dependent pathways (Pena et al., 2018; Liu and Neufeld, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lateral process motility is facilitated by turnover of actin filaments and microtubules.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that lateral process motility is facilitated by turnover of actin filaments and microtubules and may be modulated by growth factor signaling, pathways that potentially interact with neuronal activity (Georgiou et al., 1999; Lavoie-Cardinal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cytoskeletal disruption experiments.

claim: Lateral process motility may be modulated by growth factor signaling.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that lateral process motility is facilitated by turnover of actin filaments and microtubules and may be modulated by growth factor signaling, pathways that potentially interact with neuronal activity (Georgiou et al., 1999; Lavoie-Cardinal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the EGF experiments and cited literature.

claim: Much of the morphological development of Müller glia occurs when retinal waves are present.
source: Much of the morphological development of Müller glia occurs when retinal waves are present (Figure 1 and Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on temporal correlation between developmental stages and cited literature.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated that retinal waves induce increases in intracellular calcium in Müller glia.
source: Furthermore, previous studies have demonstrated that retinal waves induce increases in intracellular calcium in Müller glia (Rosa et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies did not assess whether there are distinct calcium compartments within Müller glia.
source: However, these studies did not assess whether there are distinct calcium compartments within Müller glia that could potentially have distinct impacts on lateral process motility.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in previous research.

claim: Müller glial stalks and lateral processes exhibited calcium transients in response to retinal waves.
source: Using all of these approaches, we verified that Müller glial stalks and lateral processes exhibited calcium transients in response to retinal waves as previously reported (Rosa et al., 2015), as well as spontaneous, non-wave-associated calcium transients.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data and confirms previous findings.

claim: Müller glial stalks and lateral processes exhibited spontaneous, non-wave-associated calcium transients.
source: Using all of these approaches, we verified that Müller glial stalks and lateral processes exhibited calcium transients in response to retinal waves as previously reported (Rosa et al., 2015), as well as spontaneous, non-wave-associated calcium transients.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data.

claim: Wave-associated stalk transients propagated throughout the stalk and involved many processes.
source: Wave-associated stalk transients propagated throughout the stalk and involved many processes, which we refer to as a global transient.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging observations.

claim: Lateral processes participated in some global transients but also exhibited wave-associated calcium transients independent of stalks.
source: Lateral processes participated in some global transients but also exhibited wave-associated calcium transients independent of stalks (Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A greater proportion of lateral process ROIs responded to waves than stalk ROIs.
source: Hence, lateral processes and stalks differentially participated in waves, with a greater proportion of lateral process ROIs responding to waves than stalk ROIs.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: Wave-associated calcium transients in lateral processes were consistently observed from P9 to P12.
source: In addition, wave-associated calcium transients in lateral processes were consistently observed from P9 to P12, while those in stalks were significantly reduced in terms of ΔF/F amplitude and proportion of stalks participating by P11/12 (Figures 2C and 3A; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data shown in Figures 2C and 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: Wave-associated calcium transients in stalks were significantly reduced in terms of ΔF/F amplitude and proportion of stalks participating by P11/12.
source: In addition, wave-associated calcium transients in lateral processes were consistently observed from P9 to P12, while those in stalks were significantly reduced in terms of ΔF/F amplitude and proportion of stalks participating by P11/12 (Figures 2C and 3A; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data shown in Figures 2C and 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: The subset of stalks that responded to retinal waves did so with a slight delay relative to lateral processes.
source: Finally, the subset of stalks that responded to retinal waves did so with a slight delay relative to lateral processes (Figure 2B and D; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: Müller glial stalks and lateral processes can undergo spatiotemporally distinct calcium signaling events.
source: Hence, Müller glial stalks and lateral processes can undergo spatiotemporally distinct calcium signaling events.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the calcium imaging data showing differential responses.

claim: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (mAChRs) have been implicated in Müller glial responses to retinal waves.
source: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (mAChRs) have been implicated in Müller glial responses to retinal waves (Rosa et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Isolated Müller glia undergo M1 mAChR-dependent responses to cholinergic agonists.
source: and isolated Müller glia undergo M1 mAChR-dependent responses to cholinergic agonists (Da Silva et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Bath application of pirenzepine (5 µM) led to a significant reduction in wave-associated calcium transients in stalks and lateral processes.
source: Bath application of pirenzepine (5 µM), a selective antagonist of M1 mAChRs, led to a significant reduction in wave-associated calcium transients in stalks and lateral processes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological manipulation experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The magnitude of pirenzepine's effect on wave-associated calcium transients was age- and compartment-dependent.
source: The magnitude of this effect was age- and compartment-dependent, as wave-associated transients in Müller glial stalks had greater sensitivity to M1 mAChR block at P9/10 than at P11/12, and pirenzepine sensitivity was significantly greater in stalks than in lateral processes at early ages (Figure 3B and C; Supplementary files 8–11).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Wave-associated transients in Müller glial stalks had greater sensitivity to M1 mAChR block at P9/10 than at P11/12.
source: The magnitude of this effect was age- and compartment-dependent, as wave-associated transients in Müller glial stalks had greater sensitivity to M1 mAChR block at P9/10 than at P11/12, and pirenzepine sensitivity was significantly greater in stalks than in lateral processes at early ages (Figure 3B and C; Supplementary files 8–11).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Pirenzepine sensitivity was significantly greater in stalks than in lateral processes at early ages.
source: The magnitude of this effect was age- and compartment-dependent, as wave-associated transients in Müller glial stalks had greater sensitivity to M1 mAChR block at P9/10 than at P11/12, and pirenzepine sensitivity was significantly greater in stalks than in lateral processes at early ages (Figure 3B and C; Supplementary files 8–11).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Pirenzepine-insensitive stalk responses exhibited similar amplitude and latency to those of lateral processes.
source: Pirenzepine-insensitive stalk responses exhibited similar amplitude and latency to those of lateral processes (Figure 3C and D; Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is based on analysis of pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Wave-associated responses in stalks are controlled by multiple mechanisms in addition to activation of M1 mAChRs.
source: These data suggest that wave-associated responses in stalks are controlled by multiple mechanisms in addition to activation of M1 mAChRs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of pirenzepine-insensitive responses.

claim: Pirenzepine had minimal impact on the amplitude and frequency of compound excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) and inter-wave interval (IWI).
source: Note, pirenzepine had minimal impact on the amplitude and frequency of compound excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) and inter-wave interval (IWI, Figure 3E; Supplementary file 13)
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Pirenzepine had a selective effect on Müller glial M1 mAChRs, rather than on wave-generating circuits.
source: indicating pirenzepine had a selective effect on Müller glial M1 mAChRs, rather than on wave-generating circuits.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that pirenzepine did not affect wave properties.

claim: The presence of gabazine increased the amplitude of EPSCs recorded from RGCs during retinal waves.
source: As expected, the presence of gabazine increased the amplitude of EPSCs recorded from RGCs during retinal waves (Figure 4E; Supplementary file 19).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Gabazine increased the proportion of stalks and lateral process ROIs that underwent wave-associated calcium transients.
source: Gabazine also increased the proportion of stalks and lateral process ROIs that underwent wave-associated calcium transients (Figure 4; Supplementary file 14)
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: There was a significantly larger gabazine-induced fold-change in proportion of stalks compared with lateral processes responding to waves.
source: but with differential compartment-specific effects: there was a significantly larger gabazine-induced fold-change in proportion of stalks compared with lateral processes responding to waves
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data.

claim: Gabazine led to a nearly twofold increase in the amplitude of wave-evoked fluorescence change in stalks.
source: and gabazine led to a nearly twofold increase in the amplitude of wave-evoked fluorescence change in stalks, while only slightly increasing the response amplitude in lateral processes (Figure 4C; Supplementary files 15–17).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Gabazine only slightly increased the response amplitude in lateral processes.
source: and gabazine led to a nearly twofold increase in the amplitude of wave-evoked fluorescence change in stalks, while only slightly increasing the response amplitude in lateral processes (Figure 4C; Supplementary files 15–17).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Subsequent application of pirenzepine after gabazine reduced the extent, magnitude, and latency of stalk responses to waves while largely sparing lateral process responses.
source: Subsequent application of pirenzepine reduced the extent, magnitude, and latency of stalk responses to waves while largely sparing lateral process responses (Figure 4B–D; Supplementary files 14–18)
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Pirenzepine's effect after gabazine was independent of age from P9 to P12.
source: This effect was independent of age from P9 to P12; pirenzepine suppressed wave-associated transients in stalks following gabazine-mediated upregulation of responses throughout this period.
evidence: This is based on analysis of pharmacological experiments across different ages.

claim: M1 mAChRs mediate wave-associated global calcium transients in Müller glial stalks.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that M1 mAChRs mediate wave-associated global calcium transients in Müller glial stalks
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pharmacological experiments with pirenzepine and gabazine.

claim: Stalks and lateral processes are functioning as distinct calcium compartments.
source: and support the conclusion that stalks and lateral processes are functioning as distinct calcium compartments, with lateral processes undergoing non-M1 mAChR-mediated calcium transients during retinal waves.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential pharmacological responses.

claim: Lateral processes undergo non-M1 mAChR-mediated calcium transients during retinal waves.
source: and support the conclusion that stalks and lateral processes are functioning as distinct calcium compartments, with lateral processes undergoing non-M1 mAChR-mediated calcium transients during retinal waves.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential pharmacological responses.

claim: Gabazine did not change the proportion of Müller glial processes undergoing motility.
source: Gabazine, which potentiated calcium transients in Müller glial processes and stalks, in part via activation of M1 mAChRs, did not change the proportion of processes undergoing motility.
evidence: This is based on motility imaging experiments with pharmacological manipulation.

claim: There was no significant change in lateral process motility in the presence of pirenzepine.
source: Similarly, there was no significant change in lateral process motility in the presence of pirenzepine, which blocks M1 mAChRs and preferentially abolished wave-associated calcium transients in Müller glial stalks (Figure 5A and F; see Supplementary file 20 for summary statistics).
evidence: This is based on motility imaging experiments with pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 5A and F.

claim: TBOA blocks glutamate transporters and enhances wave-associated calcium transients in Müller glia by increasing glutamate spillover.
source: TBOA blocks glutamate transporters and enhances wave-associated calcium transients in Müller glia by increasing glutamate spillover, while DNQX and AP5 block glutamatergic retinal waves and reduce calcium transients in Müller glia (Rosa et al., 2015; Blankenship et al., 2009; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: DNQX and AP5 block glutamatergic retinal waves and reduce calcium transients in Müller glia.
source: TBOA blocks glutamate transporters and enhances wave-associated calcium transients in Müller glia by increasing glutamate spillover, while DNQX and AP5 block glutamatergic retinal waves and reduce calcium transients in Müller glia (Rosa et al., 2015; Blankenship et al., 2009; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of TBOA or DNQX/AP5 had no significant impact on Müller glial lateral process motility.
source: Similar to our results in gabazine and pirenzepine, the presence of TBOA or DNQX/AP5 had no significant impact on motility (Figure 5B and F).
evidence: This is based on motility imaging experiments with pharmacological manipulation shown in Figure 5B and F.

claim: Lateral process motility does not arise from wave-associated calcium transients in stalks or processes.
source: These observations together indicate that lateral process motility does not arise from wave-associated calcium transients in stalks or processes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of effect of pharmacological manipulations on motility.

claim: Local perfusion of carbachol or glutamate onto Müller glial processes induced strong calcium transients in stalks and lateral processes.
source: In parallel experiments using retinas from Slc1a3-CreER;GCaMP6fflox mice, we confirmed that this method induced strong calcium transients in stalks and lateral processes.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments with local agonist application.

claim: Local perfusion of agonists had no impact on Müller glial lateral process motility.
source: Despite this, we observed no impact of local perfusion of agonists on Müller glial lateral process motility (Figure 5C, D and F).
evidence: This is based on motility imaging experiments with local agonist application shown in Figure 5C, D and F.

claim: BAPTA-AM blocked retinal waves and all calcium transients in Müller glia.
source: Despite blocking retinal waves and all calcium transients in Müller glia (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), the presence of BAPTA did not alter the proportion of processes exhibiting motility.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of BAPTA did not alter the proportion of Müller glial processes exhibiting motility.
source: Despite blocking retinal waves and all calcium transients in Müller glia (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), the presence of BAPTA did not alter the proportion of processes exhibiting motility.
evidence: This is based on motility imaging experiments with BAPTA-AM.

claim: Motility of Müller glial lateral processes persists in the absence of intracellular calcium transients or neuronal activity.
source: Taken together these data suggest that motility of Müller glial lateral processes persists in the absence of intracellular calcium transients or neuronal activity (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BAPTA-AM experiments shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Some observations were made using relatively small numbers of cells, and a small effect of pharmacological perturbations cannot be ruled out given sample size and high cell-to-cell variability.
source: We note however that some of these observations were made using relatively small numbers of cells, and we cannot rule out a small effect of these pharmacological perturbations given our sample size and high cell-to-cell variability in lateral process motility.
evidence: This is a caveat about the limitations of the study.

claim: During the first postnatal week, there are wave-associated calcium transients in Müller glia mediated by activation of mAChRs.
source: However, during the first postnatal week, there are wave-associated calcium transients in Müller glia also mediated by activation of mAChRs (Rosa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: β2-nAChR-KO mice exhibit significantly reduced cholinergic retinal waves.
source: β2-nAChR-KO mice exhibit significantly reduced cholinergic retinal waves (Bansal et al., 2000; Burbridge et al., 2014; McLaughlin et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: β2-nAChR-KO mice have reduced M1 mAChR-induced signaling in glial cells.
